title: You Are Lamps to the Home and Workers for the Nation!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement.
paragraphs: On 14 September 2013, a meeting of the State, district and city organisers and deputy organisers of the DMK Youth Wing was held at Anbagam in Chennai under the leadership of DMK Treasurer Thalapathi M.K. Stalin. You will have read in the newspapers that the meeting adopted four important resolutions.

The first resolution stated that the birthdays of Thanthai Periyar, the radiant sun of rationalism, and Arignar Anna, the genius of the world of knowledge, together with the day on which the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam—the star of hope of the Tamil people—was founded, are celebrated every year as Mupperum Vizha under the leadership of Kalaignar. As a continuation of that celebration, the Youth Wing resolved to carry the DMK's golden principles and the welfare schemes implemented by Kalaignar with the future well-being of the Tamil people in mind to every village and hamlet across Tamil Nadu. It also resolved to explain the degradation under Jayalalithaa's administratively incompetent Government: the collapse of law and order; murder, robbery, chain-snatching, violence and rape wherever one looked; rising prices of essential commodities; power cuts; and unemployment that caused suffering among every section of society. These matters were to be printed in simple language and distributed house to house in villages, small settlements, towns and wards, accompanied by various forms of outreach including doorstep and street-corner propaganda. As the first phase, the resolution called upon district, city, union, town, area and town-panchayat Youth Wing organisers and deputy organisers to conduct a continuous week-long State-wide campaign from 24 to 30 September 2013.

Following the resolution, Thambi Stalin, the Youth Wing Secretary, had already published the list of DMK speakers who would participate in each district. District Youth Wing organisers contacted the persons named, discussed the dates and arrangements, and confirmed when the speakers would arrive and how many meetings they would attend. Those preparations came to my attention.

Yesterday, seated at Anbagam, Thambi Stalin compiled district-wise details of the places, speakers and their arrival times and published them in today's Murasoli. The arrangements for eight districts alone had been completed; the remaining districts would follow. Those participating were not only the DMK's senior speakers. Some were speakers who had developed, and some were still developing. It was the duty of DMK members to encourage them and help them grow.

The speakers could learn what to address at these meetings from the Udanpirappu letters and question-and-answer columns that I, though above ninety years of age, sit down to write each morning—so absorbed in the work that I often take breakfast only around eleven. Many DMK speakers, including our Deputy General Secretary Duraimurugan, had told me that they copied points from my daily letters at night and found them highly useful when addressing public meetings.

The most intense political issue at present was the disproportionate-assets case involving more than ₹66 crore against Chief Minister Jayalalithaa. The case had continued for sixteen years since 1997 and had been heard in the Supreme Court, the Bengaluru Special Court and the Karnataka High Court. The accused had obtained adjournments more than a hundred times. Yet they were now approaching the Supreme Court to insist that the particular judge hearing the case must remain until it ended and that the same public prosecutor appointed by Karnataka to argue against them must continue. You have the important duty of explaining to people in every village the hidden design and selfish motive behind that demand.

I had written more than two pages about this in Murasoli on 14 September 2013. Yet Tamil and English newspapers across the State blacked out the substance. Even when they reported it, they carried no more than one or two paragraphs. If they published reports against the Government or criticism of Jayalalithaa, they would not receive full-page and half-page advertisements. Newspapers were said to earn more from government advertising than from sales. They had therefore set “journalistic ethics” aside, forgotten their democratic responsibility and concentrated on earning revenue.

The DMK has never depended upon those newspapers to conduct the movement. Even in Perarignar Anna's time, The Hindu once reported merely that “Anna too spoke at the meeting.” The DMK overcame such treatment and came to office. DMK speakers themselves undertook the work the newspapers should have done and carried public affairs to the people.

Did the newspapers' neglect mean that my views never reached the people of Tamil Nadu? When the letter on the disproportionate-assets case did not appear in the press, I wrote just four lines in Murasoli asking DMK Udanpirappus to print and distribute it as handbills. From the next day, district secretaries and leading functionaries enthusiastically began reporting how many thousands of leaflets they had printed and distributed. Youth Wing members went a step further: carrying the leaflets in their hands, they boarded buses and distributed them to the passengers. You would have seen those scenes in the press itself. Those who blacked out my letter out of fear of the rulers—like hiding the comb in a wedding house—were the ones left deceived. Speakers in the street-corner campaign must explain to the public the arguments contained in that leaflet.

Next, they must explain the daily question before Tamil Nadu: the breakdown of law and order. In my letter titled “Tamil Nadu in the Terrifying Grip of Murder,” I gathered and presented reports and opinions on the present law-and-order crisis from numerous daily newspapers and weeklies. The speakers must read out and explain, in a way ordinary people can understand, how those publications themselves criticised this Government.

On 6 September 2013, I had written an Udanpirappu letter documenting how police-station buildings constructed for the department had remained unopened while the stations continued in dilapidated premises. Only after that did officials hurriedly plead with the Chief Minister: “Karunanidhi has openly written all these truths in Murasoli; at least now give us five minutes.” After obtaining her time, they had the long-completed stations opened by video conference, and the Tamil Nadu newspapers devoted page after page to the event. Not one newspaper stated that Karunanidhi had criticised the failure to open those buildings and that only afterward did the Chief Minister allot time to inaugurate them. These facts too must be taken to the people.

I had also explained in the question-and-answer section of the 20th the history of Sudhakaran, once described as Jayalalithaa's foster son, whose extravagant wedding cost several crores; his later arrest under an AIADMK Government; the case that continued for twelve years from 2001; the judgment now delivered; and what the judge said. It serves as a clear example of how cases are filed under this Government to harass those it dislikes and to pursue political vendetta.

On 12 September 2013, I wrote in the question-and-answer section about Katchatheevu and farmers' problems. The same day, I pointed out the extraordinary case of Thanjavur Municipality issuing a tender for work that had already been completed, and the obstruction by AIADMK members of the opening of a completed bus stand in Theni.

On 8 September, I had described in some detail the great schemes implemented for women under the DMK Government. Some AIADMK ministers merely installed flex boards pretending that nothing had been done for women during DMK rule. I listed the programmes carried out for women and persons with disabilities. These too must be highlighted in the campaigns. At the same time, speakers must explain the extent to which persons with disabilities have been forced to protest during the past few days and how the police who arrest them have treated them cruelly.

They must remind people of the power-cut situation under the AIADMK Government. Those who challenged that they would solve it within three months of taking office had still failed as the third year approached. The campaign should explain how the Hogenakkal Combined Drinking Water Project had been accelerated under the DMK Government, and how it was hastily opened with great publicity under the present Government even though it was not complete, as I wrote on 6 September.

The street-corner campaign must also identify the many efforts made after the AIADMK returned to office to block major projects undertaken by the previous DMK Government for public welfare and State development. Particular attention must be drawn to the new Secretariat complex constructed at a cost exceeding ₹600 crore and left closed for three years; the fate of the Maduravoyal–Chennai Port elevated expressway; and the State Government's approach to the courts to oppose the Sethusamudram project.

One could continue writing in this manner. On 1 September itself, I clearly stated how many full-page advertisements the AIADMK Government had given the newspapers in a single week to conceal its failures and prevent their publication, and how much each newspaper received. I invited the Government to deny the figures if they were wrong and said I would accept such a denial. To this day, no answer has come. Instead, the rulers imagine that they can spend their time filing defamation cases against opposition leaders. Those conducting the week-long street-corner campaign must explain all this without omission.

The AIADMK rulers imagine that they can bask comfortably by dazzling the people with empty rhetoric, hollow statements and page after page of advertisements, creating the illusion that one achievement after another is transforming Tamil Nadu. Our responsibility is to expose that illusion with evidence in every town, street and home. I have complete faith that you—my younger brothers and sisters—will fulfil that duty. Are you not lamps to your homes and workers for the nation?
